prerequisites: Transverse and longitudinal waves
Wavelength, frequency, amplitude and phase
Reflection of waves
Interference and the principle that the resultant displacement is the sum of individual displacements
Basic wave diagrams and notation
requiredMethods: Draw successive wave positions and add their displacements graphically
Identify nodes as points of zero displacement and antinodes as points of maximum displacement
Represent string modes using loops between fixed-end nodes
Represent air-column modes using nodes and antinodes at closed and open ends
spec.depth: Students should use labelled wave diagrams and the terms node, antinode, wavelength, amplitude and mode of vibration accurately. Mathematical treatment is limited to simple wavelength relationships for string and air-column modes; derivations and advanced harmonic analysis are not required.
misconceptions: A stationary wave travels along the medium like a progressive wave; in a stationary wave the nodes and antinodes remain fixed.
Nodes have maximum displacement; nodes have zero displacement while antinodes have maximum displacement.
The distance from a node to the next node is one wavelength; it is half a wavelength.
An antinode is an end of every string; antinodes occur between adjacent nodes and depend on the mode.
An open end of an air column is a node; an open end is an antinode and a closed end is a node.
All organ pipes have the same end conditions; pipes may be open at both ends or closed at one end.
outOfScope: Detailed derivation of the superposition equation
Energy transport and power calculations for stationary waves
Doppler effect, beats and resonance beyond the formation of the stated stationary-wave modes
End correction and detailed organ-pipe acoustics
Complex harmonic spectra, Fourier analysis and advanced boundary-condition mathematics

boards.title: Graphical formation of stationary waves
boards.objective: Explain, using successive graphical positions, how two identical waves travelling in opposite directions form a stationary wave.
keyPoints: A stationary wave is formed when two waves of the same frequency, wavelength and amplitude travel through the same medium in opposite directions, usually because one wave is reflected.
Use the principle of superposition: the displacement at any point is the sum of the displacements of the two waves.
At some fixed positions the two waves always cancel, giving zero displacement; these positions are nodes.
At positions halfway between adjacent nodes, the waves reinforce and produce maximum displacement; these positions are antinodes.
The wave pattern does not move along the medium: nodes and antinodes remain at fixed positions, although the particles between them vibrate.
In a graphical method, draw the two opposite-travelling waves at successive instants and add their vertical displacements to obtain the resultant pattern.
boards.workedExample: Two equal waves meet on a stretched string. At one instant, their displacements at four points are: A: +2 cm and -2 cm; B: +1 cm and +1 cm; C: 0 cm and 0 cm; D: -1 cm and -1 cm. Add the displacements at each point: A = 0 cm, B = +2 cm, C = 0 cm, D = -2 cm. The points A and C have zero resultant displacement and are possible nodes. Points such as B and D have large resultant displacement and lie near antinodes. Repeating this construction at successive instants shows that the positions of the zero-displacement points remain fixed, so the resulting pattern is stationary rather than travelling.

boards.title: Nodes and antinodes
boards.objective: Define and distinguish nodes and antinodes in a stationary-wave pattern.
keyPoints: A node is a point in a stationary wave that always has zero displacement.
An antinode is a point in a stationary wave that has maximum displacement or maximum amplitude.
Nodes and antinodes are fixed in position.
Adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength, λ/2.
Adjacent antinodes are separated by half a wavelength, λ/2.
The distance from a node to the nearest antinode is one quarter of a wavelength, λ/4.
boards.workedExample: A stationary wave has wavelength 40 cm. The distance from a node to the next antinode is λ/4 = 40 cm ÷ 4 = 10 cm. The distance between adjacent nodes is λ/2 = 40 cm ÷ 2 = 20 cm. Therefore, the nearest antinode is 10 cm from a node, and the next node is 20 cm from that node.

boards.title: Modes of vibration of strings
boards.objective: Describe the patterns formed when a stretched string vibrates in its different modes.
keyPoints: A stretched string fixed at both ends has a node at each fixed end.
A mode of vibration is one possible stationary-wave pattern on the string.
The fundamental mode, or first harmonic, has one loop, one antinode and a node at each end; the string length is half a wavelength, L = λ/2.
The second harmonic has two loops and an additional node at the centre; L = λ.
The third harmonic has three loops and two internal nodes; L = 3λ/2.
In general, the nth harmonic has n loops and n antinodes, with nodes at both ends and L = nλ/2.
Higher modes have shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies than the fundamental mode.
boards.workedExample: A string fixed at both ends is 1.2 m long and vibrates in its second harmonic. For the second harmonic, L = λ, so λ = 1.2 m. The pattern has two loops, two antinodes and three nodes: one at each end and one at the centre. The distance between neighbouring nodes is λ/2 = 0.6 m. Thus the second-harmonic wavelength is 1.2 m and the string contains two equal loops.

boards.title: Stationary waves in air columns
boards.objective: Describe how stationary waves form in vibrating air columns in organ pipes.
keyPoints: A stationary wave in an air column forms when sound waves travelling along the column interfere with waves reflected from the end of the pipe.
At a closed end, the air cannot move, so there is a displacement node.
At an open end, the air can move with maximum displacement, so there is a displacement antinode.
An open pipe has an antinode at each end. Its fundamental mode has one half-wavelength in the pipe, so L = λ/2.
A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. Its fundamental mode has one quarter-wavelength in the pipe, so L = λ/4.
The stationary-wave pattern determines the possible modes of vibration of the air column.
boards.workedExample: An organ pipe is closed at one end and open at the other. In its fundamental mode, draw or describe a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end. The shortest pattern joining a node to an antinode is one quarter of a wavelength, so L = λ/4. If the pipe length is 0.80 m, then λ = 4L = 4 × 0.80 m = 3.20 m. Therefore, the fundamental stationary wave has wavelength 3.20 m, with a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.

checkpoint.question: Two waves of equal amplitude and frequency travel in opposite directions on a string. What is formed, and why does its pattern remain fixed?
checkpoint.answer: A stationary wave is formed because the waves interfere by superposition; nodes and antinodes remain at fixed positions.

checkpoint.question: Define a node and an antinode in a stationary wave.
checkpoint.answer: A node is a point of always-zero displacement. An antinode is a point of maximum displacement.

checkpoint.question: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic. How many loops and internal nodes are present?
checkpoint.answer: There are three loops and two internal nodes, in addition to the nodes at the two ends.

checkpoint.question: In a pipe closed at one end and open at the other, where are the displacement node and antinode in the fundamental mode?
checkpoint.answer: The displacement node is at the closed end and the displacement antinode is at the open end.

prerequisites: Potential difference and current in a circuit
Resistance and use of a resistor
Capacitor as a component that stores charge
Reading simple circuit diagrams
Using a voltmeter and ammeter safely
requiredMethods: Drawing a simple capacitor–resistor circuit
Connecting a capacitor, resistor, cell and switch in series
Observing voltage and current while the capacitor charges
Discharging the capacitor through a resistor and observing the decrease in voltage and current
Plotting or interpreting voltage/current against time
spec.depth: Students should understand and demonstrate the circuit behavior qualitatively: during charging, capacitor voltage and charge increase while current decreases; during discharging, voltage, charge and current decrease. Use simple circuit diagrams and time graphs; detailed exponential derivations and calculus are not required.
misconceptions: A capacitor allows steady direct current to flow indefinitely; in a DC charging circuit, the current falls to approximately zero after charging.
The capacitor is charged instantly; charging takes time and depends on the resistance and capacitance.
The resistor stores the charge; the capacitor stores charge, while the resistor limits current and controls the rate of charging or discharging.
Current continues in the same way during charging and discharging; its direction and behavior depend on the circuit connection.
A discharged capacitor has maximum potential difference; initially, an uncharged capacitor has approximately zero potential difference across it.
The capacitor is destroyed when it is connected to a suitable DC source; it stores energy provided its voltage rating is not exceeded.
outOfScope: Derivation of exponential charging and discharging equations
Calculus-based treatment of the time constant
Detailed capacitor construction and dielectric polarization
Series and parallel capacitor networks
Alternating-current capacitive reactance and phase relationships
Kirchhoff-law analysis beyond the simple charging and discharging circuit

boards.title: Charging a capacitor through a resistor
boards.objective: Demonstrate how a capacitor charges when connected to a DC supply through a resistor, and identify the changes in current, charge and capacitor potential difference with time.
keyPoints: Connect a cell, switch, resistor and capacitor in series, with a voltmeter across the capacitor if measurements are required.
When the switch is closed, an initially uncharged capacitor begins to charge.
At the start of charging, the capacitor potential difference is approximately zero and the current is greatest.
As charge accumulates, the potential difference across the capacitor increases and the charging current decreases.
After sufficient time, the capacitor is approximately fully charged: its potential difference is close to the supply voltage and the current is approximately zero.
The resistor limits the charging current and makes the charging process take a measurable time.
A charging graph shows capacitor potential difference increasing with time, while the current decreases with time.
boards.workedExample: Set up a 6 V cell, a 1 kΩ resistor and an initially uncharged capacitor in series. Close the switch and measure the potential difference across the capacitor at regular time intervals. At the instant of closing, record V_C ≈ 0 V and the current as maximum. Later, V_C rises toward 6 V and the current falls toward 0 A. Therefore, the demonstration shows that charging is not instantaneous: capacitor voltage increases while charging current decreases, and the final capacitor voltage is approximately the supply voltage.

boards.title: Discharging a capacitor through a resistor
boards.objective: Demonstrate how a charged capacitor discharges through a resistor and identify the changes in current, charge and potential difference with time.
keyPoints: First charge the capacitor using a DC supply; then disconnect the supply and connect the charged capacitor across a resistor.
At the beginning of discharge, the capacitor has its greatest potential difference and the discharge current is greatest.
Charge flows through the resistor in the discharge circuit, so the capacitor's stored charge and potential difference decrease with time.
The discharge current decreases as the capacitor becomes less charged and eventually becomes approximately zero.
The direction of discharge current is opposite to the charging current in the external circuit.
A discharge graph shows capacitor potential difference and current decreasing with time toward zero.
A larger resistance makes the charging or discharging process slower because it limits the current.
boards.workedExample: A capacitor is first charged to 6 V and then connected across a 1 kΩ resistor without the cell. At the instant the discharge switch is closed, the capacitor potential difference is 6 V and the initial current is I = V/R = 6/1000 = 0.006 A = 6 mA. As discharge proceeds, the capacitor voltage falls below 6 V, so I = V/R also falls; when the capacitor is effectively discharged, both voltage and current are approximately zero. Thus the resistor provides the path for discharge and limits the discharge current.

checkpoint.question: In a circuit containing a cell, resistor and initially uncharged capacitor, what happens to the capacitor potential difference and current immediately after the switch is closed and after a long time?
checkpoint.answer: Immediately after closing, the capacitor potential difference is approximately zero and the current is greatest. After a long time, the capacitor potential difference is close to the cell voltage and the current is approximately zero.

checkpoint.question: A charged 6 V capacitor is discharged through a 2 kΩ resistor. What is the initial discharge current?
checkpoint.answer: I = V/R = 6/2000 = 0.003 A = 3 mA. The current then decreases as the capacitor discharges.

checkpoint.question: Describe how to demonstrate discharging of a capacitor through a resistor.
checkpoint.answer: Charge the capacitor from a DC supply, disconnect the supply, connect the charged capacitor across a resistor, and observe that the capacitor voltage and current decrease with time toward zero.

prerequisites: Magnetic fields and electromagnetism
Electromagnetic induction: a changing magnetic field can induce an emf
Alternating current and voltage
Voltage, current, power and resistance in electrical circuits
The relationship P = VI and the idea of energy loss in cables
requiredMethods: Identify the primary and secondary coils and the core in a transformer diagram
Use the turns ratio relationship Vs/Vp = Ns/Np
Explain transformer operation as mutual induction caused by a changing magnetic flux
Use P = VI to explain why high-voltage transmission reduces current and cable losses
spec.depth: Students should know the construction, purpose of the main parts, and the sequence by which alternating current produces an induced alternating voltage. They should distinguish step-up from step-down transformers and use the basic turns-ratio relationship at an introductory mathematical level; detailed electromagnetic-field equations, transformer design, and non-ideal losses are not required.
misconceptions: A transformer cannot operate from steady direct current because its operation requires a changing magnetic field.
The primary coil is not necessarily the coil with more turns; its role is determined by which side receives the input.
A step-up transformer increases voltage but, ideally, decreases current rather than increasing both.
A step-down transformer decreases voltage and, ideally, increases current.
The iron core does not supply electrical energy; it transfers changing magnetic flux between the coils.
The voltage ratio follows the turns ratio: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, not the reverse.
High transmission voltage reduces current for a given power, so cable heating losses are reduced.
outOfScope: Detailed derivation of the transformer equations from Faraday's law
Transformer efficiency calculations and detailed causes of energy loss
Eddy-current and hysteresis-loss calculations
Complex transformer circuits and three-phase transmission
Voltage regulation, impedance matching and transformer design specifications
Operation of transformers with direct current

boards.title: Construction and operation of a transformer
boards.objective: Describe how a transformer is built and explain how alternating current produces an induced voltage in the secondary coil.
keyPoints: A transformer consists of two coils, called the primary coil and secondary coil, wound on a common laminated soft iron core.
The primary coil is connected to the alternating-current input and the secondary coil supplies the output.
The coils are electrically insulated from each other; energy is transferred through the changing magnetic field in the core.
Alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic flux in the soft iron core.
The changing magnetic flux passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating emf and voltage in it by electromagnetic induction.
A soft iron core provides a good path for magnetic flux, while laminating the core helps reduce unwanted induced currents and energy loss.
The voltage change depends on the relative numbers of turns on the primary and secondary coils.
boards.workedExample: A transformer has an alternating-current supply connected to its primary coil. The primary coil produces a changing magnetic field in the laminated soft iron core. This changing flux links the secondary coil, so an alternating emf is induced across the secondary coil. The coils are not electrically connected; the energy is transferred by mutual induction through the core.

boards.title: Step-up and step-down transmission
boards.objective: Describe how step-up and step-down transformers are used to transfer electricity efficiently along cables.
keyPoints: A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil: Ns > Np. It increases the output voltage.
A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil: Ns < Np. It decreases the output voltage.
For an ideal transformer, the voltage ratio is related to the turns ratio: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
For an ideal transformer, input power is approximately equal to output power: VpIp ≈ VsIs. Therefore, increasing voltage reduces current for the same transmitted power.
Electricity is stepped up to a high voltage before transmission along cables.
For a given transmitted power, the high voltage means a smaller current in the cables.
Cable heating loss is proportional to I²R, so reducing the current greatly reduces energy loss during transmission.
Near consumers, a step-down transformer reduces the high transmission voltage to a safer, useful voltage.
boards.workedExample: A transformer raises the transmission voltage from 25 kV to 250 kV. For the same transmitted power, use P = VI: I2/I1 = V1/V2 = 25/250 = 0.10. Thus the transmission current becomes one-tenth of its original value. Since cable heating loss is proportional to I²R, the loss becomes (0.10)² = 0.01 of the original loss, or 1%. This is why a step-up transformer makes transmission more efficient. A step-down transformer can then reduce the voltage near consumers.

checkpoint.question: A transformer has two coils wound on a laminated soft iron core. What is the function of the changing current in the primary coil?
checkpoint.answer: It produces changing magnetic flux in the core, which induces an alternating emf in the secondary coil by mutual induction.

checkpoint.question: Why is a step-up transformer used before electricity is transmitted along cables?
checkpoint.answer: It increases the voltage, so for the same transmitted power the current is lower. The lower current reduces cable heating loss, which is proportional to I²R.

prerequisites: The electromagnetic spectrum includes radio waves through to gamma rays.
Different types of electromagnetic radiation have different frequencies, wavelengths and energies.
Gamma rays and X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation.
requiredMethods: Link the biological effect of radiation to its ability to ionise atoms and damage cells or DNA.
Match a type of radiation with an appropriate medical use and explain the purpose of that use.
spec.depth: Students should describe the main harmful biological effects of ionising radiation and its principal medical uses using accurate everyday scientific vocabulary. No quantitative dose calculations, detailed cellular mechanisms, or treatment planning are required.
misconceptions: All radiation is equally harmful; biological damage depends on the type, energy and exposure of the radiation.
Radiation makes a person radioactive in every situation; exposure to X-rays does not normally make the person radioactive.
Radiotherapy is used only for diagnosis; it uses high-energy radiation to damage and destroy cancer cells.
Medical uses of radiation have no risks; excessive or unnecessary exposure can damage healthy tissue.
Gamma rays and X-rays are identical in origin and use, although both are ionising electromagnetic radiation.
outOfScope: Detailed molecular mechanisms of DNA repair and mutation.
Radiation dose calculations, absorbed dose, equivalent dose and dose limits.
Nuclear decay equations, half-life calculations and nuclear reactor operation.
Detailed radiotherapy treatment planning and radiation shielding calculations.
Non-ionising radiation effects such as the detailed thermal effects of microwaves or infrared radiation.

boards.title: How radiation affects living tissue
boards.objective: Describe the biological effects of ionising radiation on cells, tissues and the body.
keyPoints: Ionising radiation has enough energy to remove electrons from atoms and molecules.
Ionisation can damage molecules in cells, including DNA.
Damage to DNA may cause mutations; mutations can contribute to the development of cancer.
Large or intense exposure can kill cells and damage tissues, producing harmful effects such as burns or tissue injury.
The biological effect depends on the type and energy of the radiation, the exposure received and which tissue is exposed.
Radiation can also damage rapidly dividing cells, which is relevant to both harmful effects and medical treatment.

boards.title: Radiation in medicine
boards.objective: Describe how radiation is used for medical imaging, treatment and tracing processes in the body.
keyPoints: X-rays pass through the body to different extents and are used to produce images of internal structures, especially bones.
Gamma rays can be used in radiotherapy to damage and destroy cancer cells.
Radiotherapy must be directed carefully because it can also damage healthy cells.
Radioactive tracers can be introduced into the body in controlled amounts and detected to show the function or location of organs and tissues.
The medical benefit of radiation must be balanced against the risk of damage to healthy tissue.
Radiation is used under controlled conditions and with appropriate protection to reduce unnecessary exposure.

checkpoint.question: State one harmful biological effect of ionising radiation and one medical use of radiation.
checkpoint.answer: Ionising radiation can damage DNA and cause mutations or cancer. X-rays can be used for medical imaging, or gamma rays can be used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells.

spec.depth: Students should apply standard English proofreading and editing at sentence and short-text level. They should use basic grammatical terms and correct common structural, agreement, function-word and spelling errors without advanced grammatical analysis.
misconceptions: Thinking that proofreading means checking spelling only.
Changing a sentence's meaning while editing it.
Choosing the verb form according to the nearest noun instead of the actual subject.
Assuming that a long group of words is automatically a complete sentence.
Treating punctuation alone as a correction for every run-on sentence.
Confusing function words such as articles, prepositions, pronouns and conjunctions.
Using a spelling that sounds correct without checking the word's standard form.

boards.title: A systematic proofreading routine
boards.objective: Proofread and edit own, peers' and given text by locating and correcting errors without changing the intended meaning.
keyPoints: Proofreading is careful checking of written text for errors.
Editing includes identifying an error, deciding the required correction and rewriting the text accurately.
Use separate checks for sentence structure, subject-verb agreement, function words and spelling.
Read the text once for meaning and again for individual errors.
Check own writing, a peer's writing and a supplied passage using the same careful process.
boards.workedExample: Given text: "The students was preparing there notes, but one student forget to bring his book." Step 1, read for meaning. Step 2, check structure and agreement: change "was" to "were" because "students" is plural. Step 3, check function and spelling: change "there" to "their" and "forget" to "forgot". Corrected text: "The students were preparing their notes, but one student forgot to bring his book."

boards.title: Building complete sentences
boards.objective: Correct faulty sentence structure in given sentences.
keyPoints: A complete sentence should express a complete thought.
A sentence normally requires a subject and a verb.
Correct sentence fragments by supplying or joining the missing part when the intended meaning is clear.
Correct run-on sentences by separating complete thoughts or joining them appropriately.
Keep the original meaning while making the sentence grammatically complete and clear.
boards.workedExample: Faulty sentence: "Because the road was flooded." This is a fragment because it does not express a complete thought. Correction: "The bus was late because the road was flooded." Faulty sentence: "The bell rang the students left the room." This is a run-on sentence. Correction: "The bell rang, and the students left the room."

boards.title: Matching subjects and verbs
boards.objective: Correct subject-verb agreement errors in sentences.
keyPoints: The verb must agree with its subject in number.
A singular subject takes a singular verb in the present tense; a plural subject takes a plural verb.
Do not choose the verb according to a noun placed between the subject and the verb.
Identify the main subject first, then select the correct verb form.
Check agreement in both original writing and edited text.
boards.workedExample: Faulty sentence: "The group of players are practicing." The subject is "group," which is singular; "of players" is a modifying phrase. Correct sentence: "The group of players is practicing." Another example: "The players in the group is practicing" is corrected to "The players in the group are practicing" because the subject "players" is plural.

boards.title: Checking function and spelling
boards.objective: Correct errors in the use of function words and in spelling.
keyPoints: Function words help show grammatical relationships and include common articles, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions and auxiliary words.
Select the function word that fits the sentence's meaning and grammatical structure.
Check commonly confused words in context rather than choosing only by sound.
Correct misspelled words using the standard spelling required by the sentence.
After correction, reread the whole sentence to ensure that it is both grammatical and meaningful.
boards.workedExample: Faulty sentence: "She went too the library and borrowed a book about grammer." The function word "too" is incorrect; the required preposition is "to." The spelling "grammer" is incorrect; the standard spelling is "grammar." Correct sentence: "She went to the library and borrowed a book about grammar."
